title: The hands-on slot
objective: See where a browser lab sits in a lesson, and how it takes over the screen when you actually start working in it.

blocks.text: A lab is the one thing that genuinely belongs embedded. It is not something to read — it is somewhere to work, and it has to be inside the lesson so that finishing it can count towards your progress.

In the flow of the lesson it sits at a comfortable size, so you can see it alongside the instructions. The moment you start typing in it, that size stops being enough — which is what the expand control is for.
Not every hands-on moment deserves a full workspace. A two-minute check belongs right here in the reading, because making someone open a separate environment for it is the reason they skip it.

blocks.title: Check who owns this file
blocks.description: One command, one answer. Small enough to do without leaving the sentence you were reading.

blocks.title: Read and fix a permission problem
blocks.description: A throwaway machine with a file the wrong people can write to. Find it and fix it. This one needs room to work, so it can fill the screen.

blocks.title: Why this is the trust mechanism
blocks.text: A quiz shows you can recognise the right answer. A lab shows you can produce it. That is what makes a required checkpoint worth requiring, and what lets someone skip other lessons with confidence.

blocks.title: What to check in this demo
steps: Press Expand to full screen and confirm the panel fills the window
Press Escape and confirm you land back where you were
Resize the browser narrow and check the panel still behaves
blocks.expected: The panel grows to the full window with a clear way out, and shrinking the window does not break the layout.

cheatsheet: A lab is embedded because it is somewhere to work, not something to read
Inline at a readable size, full screen when you are actually working
Escape always returns you to the lesson at the same place
Doing beats recognising — the lab is what makes a required checkpoint meaningful

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a lab embedded when an article is not?

choices.B: A lab is somewhere the learner works, and completing it has to count towards progress — an article is something they read, which is better as native page content
choices.D: Articles are not part of courses

checkpoint.explanation: The split is doing versus reading. Anything interactive that feeds progress stays inside; anything to read becomes part of the page itself.

checkpoint.prompt: What should happen when the learner leaves full screen?

choices.A: They return to the course map
choices.C: They land back in the lesson at the same place

checkpoint.explanation: Losing your place is the thing that actually breaks flow. Expanding and collapsing must never cost the learner their position.

checkpoint.prompt: Which content types get a full-screen control?

choices.B: Only things you look at closely or work inside — diagrams, video and labs
choices.D: Nothing, full screen is never useful

checkpoint.explanation: Full screen is an escape hatch for detail and for work. Needing it to make a document readable is a sign that document should not have been embedded.
